items.title: Newly identified protein pathway helps HIV stay hidden despite treatment
items.summary: Current HIV medicines are effective at suppressing the virus in the blood. However, HIV can remain "asleep" or dormant inside certain immune cells and in the brain. These hidden pockets of virus, called HIV reservoirs, are the main reason HIV cannot be cured with today's treatments.

items.title: Nanoscale alloy redesign tackles cold brittleness for potential deep-space and deep-sea applications
items.summary: Metallic materials used in extremely cold environments must maintain high strength, ductility and fracture toughness to support applications in aerospace, clean energy, superconducting systems and deep-space exploration. items.title: Seabird family tree predicts which species accumulate plastic better than diet, global analysis finds
items.summary: What seabirds eat might seem like a good starting point for identifying species that tend to accumulate plastic in their digestive systems. Yet a recent global analysis suggests that mapping the evolutionary relatives of birds could offer better clues than their diets or feeding methods alone.

items.title: Could lowering high blood pressure be as simple as stimulating your ear?

items.title: A hidden bias in human language challenges 70 years of science
items.summary: A groundbreaking study challenges 70 years of assumptions about how human language works. items.title: Ancient stalagmites reveal exceptions to Asia–South America monsoon seesaw over the past 450,000 years
items.summary: In places like South Asia, Africa and parts of the Americas, monsoon rains supply water for drinking, crops and hydropower for billions of people. items.title: NASA’s asteroid Bennu samples reveal a 4.5-billion-year-old secret
items.summary: Tiny samples from asteroid Bennu are rewriting scientists' understanding of how our Solar System formed. New evidence suggests that Bennu was born where material from the inner and outer Solar System mixed, with Jupiter playing a surprising role in shaping its formation.

items.summary: The Sun’s seemingly peaceful regions are hiding a surprisingly complex magnetic world. items.title: Cleaner brick kilns cut pollution, but gains did not reach workers, research finds
items.summary: Relatively simple changes to the way traditional brick kilns operate in Bangladesh can reduce pollution, save fuel and improve the quality of bricks they produce.

items.title: New long‑clawed British dinosaur is the first of its kind in Europe
items.summary: The fossilized skull of a new species of mysterious meat-eating dinosaur from the Isle of Wight has been rediscovered in the collections of the Natural History Museum after over 100 years in storage.

items.title: Swinging virtual lightsabers and punching improve pattern-based learning in VR tests
items.summary: Punching a virtual response box or swinging a virtual lightsaber can dramatically improve learning on certain tasks, according to new research from Florida Atlantic University's College of Engineering and Computer Science, which challenges long-standing assumptions about how people learn.

items.title: Typhoon Champi knocks out power to thousands in Taiwan
items.summary: Emergency crews scrambled on Saturday to restore power to tens of thousands of homes in Taiwan after Typhoon Champi's fierce winds battered the island, with the storm moving toward China and Japan.

items.title: NASA adopting Apollo's urgency to build a moon base and land astronauts within 2 years

items.title: Power cuts and sleep: Students link load shedding to anxiety, disrupted rest and lower grades
items.summary: South Africa endured its worst year of load shedding (scheduled power cuts by the country's utility, Eskom) in 2023. The power went off on 335 of the year's 365 days, often several times a day. Since then, the country has gone more than a year and a half without these planned power cuts.

items.summary: When heavy rain hits a city, knowing where water will accumulate is only part of the picture. Who lives in the affected buildings? How might flooding disrupt their lives? And where could additional support make the greatest difference?

items.title: Counting magnetic flux quanta offers new way to measure photon numbers
items.summary: Researchers at AIST have directly observed magnetic flux quanta generated in a superconductor by photon absorption and demonstrated a new principle of photon detection that identifies the number of photons based on the number of these flux quanta.

items.title: 'It's pretty toxic… but just a little, I want to be like that': What young men think of manosphere content
items.summary: Masculinity content promises young men self-optimization and success, but often delivers health harms, risk-taking, unattainable standards, gender stereotypes and misogyny. The latter is the strongest predictor of violent extremism.

items.title: Chemically modified sugars enable direct nanostructure formation
items.summary: Researchers at AIST have demonstrated the synthesis of nanoporous carbonaceous materials and carbonaceous materials with layered nanostructures through a simple process involving the chemical modification of common sugars such as sucrose and fructose.

items.title: The psychology of why we overpay for used cars—study points to left-digit bias
items.summary: Consumers routinely ignore information when making purchases. They overlook the tax attached to a price, skim past ingredient lists and often fail to process exact numbers with any precision.

items.summary: Establishing a long-term presence on the moon will require solving challenges that are easy to overlook on Earth. Lunar temperatures, for instance, can vary from hundreds of degrees below zero to boiling, making effective insulation essential for lunar habitats.

items.summary: Research shows that crises do more than cause financial market volatility and falling share prices—they lead to markets becoming far more interconnected.

items.title: Black holes spinning near maximum rate could split in two, calculations suggest
items.summary: Two black holes can collide and merge into one. But could the opposite happen: could a single black hole split into two smaller ones? That question is explored in a new theoretical study: "When Black Holes Admit Pair-of-pants Topologies," published in the journal Physical Review D.

items.title: Hoarders without borders: Study suggests investors aid international expansion
items.summary: Venture capital firms can help young businesses expand internationally by providing funding as well as market knowledge, expertise and access to professional networks, according to a research literature review published in the International Journal of Management and Enterprise Development.

items.title: From sea anemone to human fertility: A new research organism for understanding meiosis
items.summary: Every egg cell and sperm cell depends on meiosis, a tightly choreographed process in which chromosomes find their partners, exchange genetic material and then divide. When meiosis goes awry in humans, the consequences can include infertility, miscarriage and birth defects.

items.title: An ancient virus in chimpanzee DNA switches off a gene that is active in humans
items.summary: Humans and chimpanzees share almost all their genes. Despite this, our brains have developed in different ways. Researchers at Lund University in Sweden have now shown that a viral pandemic dating back several million years is likely to be part of the explanation.
